items.prompt: Tap every square the white rook on d4 attacks. A square holding the rook's own piece counts too: the rook defends that piece.

claims.statement: The piece on d4 attacks exactly these squares.
A black pawn stands on d7.
A black knight stands on g4.
A white pawn stands on b4.

hints: Go one direction at a time: up, down, left, right.
On each line the rook reaches every square up to and including the first piece it meets. Nothing behind that piece is attacked.
Up the d-file it stops at the black pawn on d7. To the left it stops at its own pawn on b4. To the right it stops at the black knight.
items.explain: The rook attacks up to and including the first piece on each line: the black pawn on d7, the black knight on g4, and its own pawn on b4 (which it defends). The squares behind them, d8, h4 and a4, are not attacked.

items.prompt: Tap every square the white bishop on c3 attacks. Count the square of a piece of its own side too (the bishop defends it).

claims.statement: The piece on c3 attacks exactly these squares.
A white pawn stands on e5.
A black knight stands on a5.

hints: Take the four diagonals one at a time.
On each diagonal the bishop reaches every square up to and including the first piece it meets.
Toward the e-file it stops at its own pawn on e5. Toward the a-file it stops at the black knight.
items.explain: Up and to the right the bishop reaches d4, then its own pawn on e5 (defended), and stops. Up and to the left it reaches b4, then the black knight on a5. Down it runs to a1 and e1.

items.prompt: The white pawn on e4 is blocked by the black pawn on e5. Tap every square the e4 pawn attacks.

claims.statement: The piece on e4 attacks exactly these squares.
A black knight stands on d5.
The pawn's only legal move is the capture on d5.

hints: A pawn moves straight ahead but captures in a different direction.
Think of the two squares diagonally in front of the pawn.
They are the squares on the d-file and the f-file one rank up. The block on e5 does not change them.
items.explain: A pawn attacks the two squares diagonally ahead, here d5 and f5, whether or not it is blocked. The black knight on d5 is attacked. The pawn's only legal move is to capture on d5; the square straight ahead, e5, is not attacked.

items.prompt: Tap every square the white knight on d4 attacks. Pieces stand next to it; does that matter?

claims.statement: The piece on d4 attacks exactly these squares.
A white pawn stands on c2.
A black pawn stands on e6.

hints: A knight attacks the eight squares that are an L-shape away.
A knight jumps, so the pieces beside it are not in its way.
Two of the eight squares hold a pawn of its own side or an enemy pawn; they still count.
items.explain: A knight jumps, so the pawns on d3 and d5 beside it do not block it. It attacks eight squares: b3, b5, c2, c6, e2, e6, f3 and f5. Its own pawn on c2 is defended by it, and the black pawn on e6 is attacked.

items.prompt: The black bishop on d5 is defended by the pawn on e6. Is it attacked by the white rook on d1? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: One white piece, the rook, attacks d5.
One black piece, the pawn on e6, defends d5.
The rook attacks d5 along the open d-file.

hints: Ask only whether the rook attacks the bishop. Do not think about the pawn yet.
Look along the d-file from d1.
Nothing stands between the rook and the bishop. The pawn on e6 only makes the bishop defended.
items.explain: The rook attacks the bishop along the open d-file, and the pawn on e6 defends the bishop. Attacked and defended are separate facts; a piece can be both.

items.prompt: Black to move. The white knight on c4 is pinned to its king, so White cannot move it. Can the black king still step to e5? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The pinned knight has no legal move.
The knight on c4 attacks e5.
The king may go to six squares, and e5 is not one of them.

hints: Which white pieces attack e5?
The knight cannot move. Does that stop it from attacking?
A piece that is pinned to its own king still attacks squares; a king may not step onto a square an enemy piece attacks.
items.explain: The knight on c4 is pinned by the bishop on e6, so it has no legal move, yet it still attacks e5. The black king may not step onto an attacked square, so e5 is not available to it.

items.prompt: Does the white pawn on d4 attack the black knight? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: One white pawn attacks e5.
Only that pawn attacks e5.
The d4 pawn attacks c5 and e5.

hints: Where does a white pawn on d4 attack?
Look at the two squares diagonally ahead of the pawn.
e5 is one of them.
items.explain: A pawn attacks the squares diagonally ahead. From d4 those are c5 and e5, and the knight stands on e5.

items.prompt: Does the white pawn on d4 attack the black knight? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: No white pawn attacks d5.
No white piece attacks d5.
The d4 pawn attacks c5 and e5, not d5.

hints: Where does a white pawn on d4 attack?
Look at the two squares diagonally ahead of the pawn.
The knight stands straight ahead, on d5. Is d5 diagonal?
items.explain: The knight stands straight in front of the pawn. A pawn attacks only the diagonal squares, so the knight on d5 is not attacked by it.

items.prompt: Does the white pawn on d4 attack the black knight? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: One white pawn attacks e5.
The blocked pawn cannot advance; its only legal move is the capture on e5.
The d4 pawn attacks c5 and e5.

hints: Where does a white pawn on d4 attack?
A black pawn now stands in front of it. Does that change the diagonals?
The pawn is blocked and cannot move, but its attack squares are the same.
items.explain: A black pawn blocks the d4 pawn, so it cannot advance. Its attack squares are still c5 and e5, so it can still capture the knight on e5. Being blocked does not switch an attack off.

items.prompt: Tap every square the black bishop on f6 attacks. A square holding the bishop's own piece counts too: the bishop defends that piece.

claims.statement: The piece on f6 attacks exactly these squares.
A white pawn stands on b2.

hints: Take the four diagonals through f6 one at a time.
On each diagonal stop at the first piece, and count that piece's square.
Two diagonals run toward White's side of the board, two toward Black's own pieces.
items.explain: Down the long diagonal the bishop runs through e5, d4 and c3 and stops at the white pawn on b2. It also reaches g5 and h4, and e7. It defends its own queen on d8 and its own pawn on g7.

items.prompt: Is the black queen on d8 attacked by the white rook on d1? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: No white piece attacks d8.
The rook reaches the pawn on d5 and nothing beyond it.
A black pawn stands on d5.

hints: Look along the d-file from d1 toward d8.
Is there a piece between the rook and the queen?
The rook meets the pawn on d5 first. That pawn is attacked; the queen behind it is not.
items.explain: The rook attacks the black pawn on d5, the first piece on the d-file, and nothing behind it. The queen on d8 is not attacked until the pawn leaves the file.
